For researchers

Sources & method

Recording provenance, the evidence behind a claim, and the difference between a written bar and a measured time.

MethodRecordingsDossiersScoresDownloadsCitation

How claims are labelled

Evidence belongs to each field

Documented
Stated in a cited source. This identifies the source’s claim; it does not guarantee that the source is right.
Inferred
Estimated from the evidence, not explicitly documented. The note gives the reasoning.
Disputed
Sources disagree. The dossier retains the alternatives and their sources.
Unknown
Not established from the sources consulted. An upload date is not a session date; an uploader is not necessarily a performer or transfer engineer.
Not applicable
The field does not apply. This is not a substitute for ‘unknown’.

What a cue time means

score-aligned
A written bar is matched to its performed occurrence in this recording. Repeats are counted separately.
score-proportion
Placement estimated from the score’s proportions. Tempo changes and pauses can move the event away from the estimated time.
audio-feature
A measured feature of this recording, such as a silence or a level change, locates the event. It does not by itself identify a chord or instrument.
documented
A fact from a cited source; it need not identify an audible event at that second.
general
A description of the surrounding stretch, not a claim about one instant.

Provisional alignment

A machine has matched score events to the recording; a named listener has not yet checked the published alignment against the score. A provisional bar time is an estimate, not an exact onset. ‘Reviewed’ records a listening check, with its scope and reviewer in the score data. Cue precision distinguishes a moment (about ±2 seconds) from a passage; neither label removes uncertainty in the underlying alignment.

Rights statements report the sources and their qualifications, not worldwide legal clearance. The composition, edition, performance, recording and digital transfer can have different rights.

US status is not established and no worldwide clearance is claimed. The Archive’s Public Domain Mark is an assertion, not an ownership release; the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not relied upon. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

Anton Bruckner · Symphony No. 7 in E major, WAB 107 · III. Scherzo — Sehr schnell; Trio — Etwas langsamer

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Hochschulsymphonieorchester (Munich) (orchestra), Marcus Bosch (conductor) Documented

The IMSLP performance entry gives “Hochschulsymphonieorchester (Munich), Marcus Bosch (conductor)”, the MP3’s embedded artist tag reads “Hochschulsymphonieorchester (München), Ltg. Marcus Bosch”, and the Munich analysis page repeats the credit. The Commons page credits only “University of Music and Theatre Munich” as author. No roster of players is given.

[2] [3] [5] [1]
Work version
Unknown Unknown

Neither the Commons page, the IMSLP performance entry, the embedded tags nor the Munich analysis page names the edition performed (Gutmann 1885, Haas, Nowak or Cohrs). The 1885 first edition is cited only as a viewable public-domain score for the orchestration timeline.

[1] [2] [5]
Recorded
2020 (credits) or 8 November 2021 (inferred from file names and a programme listing) Disputed: sources disagree

The credits (IMSLP: “Live recording at the University of Music and Theatre Munich 2020”; embedded date tag; Commons; Munich analysis page) give 2020. The IMSLP file names, however, carry the token 2021-11-08, and the Gasteig November 2021 programme lists a Hochschulsymphonieorchester München concert under Marcus Bosch with Bruckner’s Seventh at the Isarphilharmonie, 19:00, under Mo 08. That matching concert is an inferred association, not proof that the files were cut from it; neither date is promoted to a settled session date, and no day or month is documented in the credits.

  • 2020 (year only; credit on IMSLP, Commons, the embedded tags and the Munich analysis page)
  • 8 November 2021 (inferred from the IMSLP file-name token 2021-11-08 and the Gasteig programme listing)
[2] [3] [1] [5] [6]
Place
University of Music and Theatre Munich (Hochschule für Musik und Theater München); the hall is not named in the credits Documented

IMSLP’s miscellaneous note and the embedded comment (“Live-Konzertmitschnitt der Hochschule für Musik und Theater München 2020”) name the institution as the place of the live recording, not a hall. The Gasteig programme lists a concert with the same forces at the Isarphilharmonie; whether the recording was made there is not established.

[2] [3] [6]

University of Music and Theatre Munich (IMSLP publisher information); no commercial label Documented

IMSLP’s publisher field reads “University of Music and Theatre Munich, 2020”. The file is a concert recording distributed through IMSLP and Wikimedia Commons, not a label release.

[1] [5]
Recording rights
US-government sound recording: Commons explicitly applies PD-USGov-Military-Marines to the performance/recording Documented

Rule 1, recording-specific US-law basis under 17 USC §105, not worldwide CC clearance. Commons separates Performance/Recording from Composition and attributes the file to a Marine Band official-duty recording with an official .mil source. No CC-NC licence appears in the Commons record or the reviewed official source wording. Marine Band boilerplate says its institutionally distributed recordings ‘may not be distributed for private use and are not for sale’ because appropriated funds are used: this is the agency’s physical-distribution policy, not a non-commercial copyright licence on the government performance. Official web downloads are offered separately. Direct upstream retrieval returned HTTP 403 during this research; the official page’s indexed distribution wording and reader-accessible download instructions were examined, and the file’s recording-specific Commons declaration remains explicit. No claim of worldwide rights or a cleared private arrangement is made.

[1]
Composition rights
Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain. Inferred, not documented

A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

[10] [7] [11] [3] [4] [5]
Recording rights
Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established. Inferred, not documented

Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

The Sibley Music Library marks its early printed orchestral score, including Rückert’s text, as public domain. Documented

The catalogue gives Mahler’s dates as 1860–1911 and Rückert’s as 1788–1866. This refers to the historical composition and text, not an unidentified modern performing edition; the catalogue’s inconsistent publication year is not adopted.

[1] [5]
Work version
Unknown Unknown

The source identifies the orchestral song, but not its performing edition or editorial alterations. The listening notes use the low-voice orchestral score, C. F. Kahnt plate 4460, for passage-level scoring; they do not claim this exact printed edition was on the performers’ desks. In this transfer, songs IV–V have late pitch-class profiles about a semitone above the written score and the Fischer-Dieskau transfer. The cause—speed, transposition or other processing—has not been established. No tuning correction or numerical tempo comparison is asserted.

DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).

Sergei Rachmaninoff · Sérénade, Op. 3 No. 5 · Sostenuto — Tempo di Valse

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Sergei Rachmaninoff (piano) Documented[1] [3] [4]
Work version
Original (1892) version of the Sérénade, as played by the composer in 1922; performing text not identified Inferred, not documented

Wikipedia’s list of the composer’s recordings labels the 4 November 1922 recording the 1892 version, and the 1940 revised version was published only in 1940 (Henle). IMSLP’s page says No. 5 was revised in 1922; the Henle report documents the revised text as Charles Foley’s 1940 edition, so that remark is not followed. Henle also states that the composer’s own recording diverges from the printed notation of the original version in many places. Henle does not identify which composer recording it means; the cited original score is therefore not assumed to be a literal transcript of the 1922 performance.

Recording rights
Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis). Documented

Commons supplies only composition-level PD-old-70; its description says November 1956, its filename says November 1959, and the dossier preserves an unexplained 1954 embedded date. All three attributions precede 1963. The opened Fricsay/RIAS commercial-carrier listing also documents French 1955 and German 1958 editions, but has not been matched to this transfer and does not settle its session. Usable under the programme’s pre-1963 European sound-recording rule; the former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US sound-recording status is not established. A recording date alone is not represented as an independently verified first-publication date.

[1]
Work version
Original solo-piano version (1904–05) Documented

The Commons description calls this the second movement of Ravel’s Miroirs “for piano”. No performing edition is named; the first edition (Demets, 1906) was used only to describe the written music, and is not stated to be the performer’s edition.

2014-04-01 Documented

No hall or studio is named, so the place is an inference.

Recording rights
Rule 1 — recording-specific public-domain release: PD-USGov-Military-Army (US-law basis). Documented

Commons expressly applies PD-USGov-Military-Army to the recording or official federal-government performance, not only to the composition. Under 17 U.S.C. § 105(a), official US Government works are not protected by US copyright. This is rule 1’s recording-specific public-domain release route, not rule 2’s publication-date route; it does not establish worldwide public-domain status.

Rule 1 — recording-specific public-domain release: PD-USGov-Military-Marines (US-law basis). Documented

Commons expressly applies PD-USGov-Military-Marines to the recording or official federal-government performance, not only to the composition. Further reading

  • Timothy Day, A Century of Recorded Music: Listening to Musical History (Yale University Press, 2002 paperback).recording-history

    Examines how recording changed both listening and musical performance.

  • Mark Katz, Capturing Sound (University of California Press, 2010 edition).recording-history

    Studies the effects of recording technology on music-making and listening.

  • Robert Philip, Performing Music in the Age of Recording (Yale University Press, 2004).recording-history

    Studies recorded performance as evidence of changing musical practice, rather than treating recordings only as editions to collect.

Further reading

  • Clive Brown, Classical and Romantic Performing Practice, second edition (Oxford University Press, 2025).study

    Historical performing conventions in Classical and Romantic repertory; the linked scholarly review identifies the second edition.

  • John Butt, Playing with History: The Historical Approach to Musical Performance (Cambridge University Press, 2002).study

    Examines the intellectual claims of historically informed performance, including authenticity, intention, modernism and postmodernism.

  • Robert Philip, Performing Music in the Age of Recording (Yale University Press, 2004).recording-history

    Studies recorded performance as evidence of changing musical practice, rather than treating recordings only as editions to collect.
